q.t: In Class 8, science is mainly about…
q.e: Class 6: wonder; Class 7: evolves; Class 8: investigates.

q.t: The goal this year is to learn…
q.e: Learning how to investigate matters more than facts.

q.t: In the book's pictures, the root stands for…
q.e: The root is the solid foundation; the kite is curiosity.

q.t: The kite stands for…
q.e: Investigation needs both root and kite.

q.t: The most important rule in experimenting is to…
o: Change one thing at a time
q.e: Then any difference can be blamed on that one thing.

q.t: Which is a testable question?
o: What changes the way a puri puffs up?
q.e: An experiment could answer it.

q.t: Can a kitchen be a place to do science?
q.e: You don't need a laboratory.

q.t: 'How long did the puri take to puff?' gives an observation that is…
q.e: Numbers let you compare how much.

q.t: Why keep notes on everything?
o: To answer questions you hadn't thought of and let others repeat it
q.e: Notes record surprises and make experiments repeatable.

q.t: Do scientists fully understand why a puri puffs?
q.e: An everyday question isn't necessarily easy or answered.

q.t: In the puri experiment, oil temperature is something you…
q.e: It's one of the variables you control.

q.t: 'Did it puff?' is something you…
q.e: It's the result you observe.

q.t: To test oil temperature, dough circles should have…
o: Same thickness, flour and dropping method
q.e: Keep everything else the same.

q.t: If you change thickness AND flour together, you…
o: Can't tell which caused the result
q.e: Two changes at once hide the cause.

q.t: Why are numbers more useful than yes/no observations?
o: They let you compare how much
q.e: 'Took 5 s vs 12 s' tells more than 'puffed vs puffed'.

q.t: Observation without imagination…
q.e: You need both root and kite.

q.t: Imagination without observation…
o: Never checks if the answer is true
q.e: Ideas must be tested against what you see.

q.t: The investigation cycle is…
q.e: Results raise new questions.

q.t: Which habit is first in the list?
o: Start from something you actually noticed
q.e: Real investigations start from real observations.

q.t: Why does this book's chapter order matter?
o: The chapters connect as a chain
q.e: Electricity → forces → pressure → weather → particles.

q.t: Testing the effect of flour type, what must stay the same?
o: Thickness, size, oil temperature, dropping method
q.e: Vary one thing; keep the rest fixed.

q.t: A student tests puri size and oil temperature at once and says 'size matters'. What's wrong?
o: Two things changed — can't tell which mattered
q.e: Change one thing at a time.

q.t: Which list is all things you CONTROL in the puri test?
q.e: Puffing time and yes/no are observations.

q.t: Why record the smell and splatter even when testing temperature?
o: They might answer questions you hadn't thought of
q.e: Notes catch surprises.

q.t: Sharpening a question means…
o: Making it specific enough for an experiment to settle
q.e: 'What changes puffing?' not 'why is cooking interesting?'

q.t: Which chapter question is 'Why does sugar disappear into tea?'
q.e: Chapter 9.

q.t: Which chapter asks 'How did watching the Moon give us calendars?'
q.e: Chapter 11.

q.t: A good experiment lets someone else…
q.e: Clear notes make experiments repeatable.

q.t: Weather leads to asking what air is made of. Which chapter follows?
q.e: The chain of connections.

q.t: Why expect an answer to produce a better question?
o: Each answer opens new things to investigate
q.e: That's how science moves forward.

q.t: You want to know if a seed's soaking time affects how fast it sprouts. What do you vary?
q.e: One variable at a time.

q.t: In that seed test, what do you measure?
q.e: That's the outcome you observe.

q.t: Which question can an experiment settle?
o: Does salt make water boil at a different temperature?
q.e: It's specific and measurable.

q.t: Two puris at different oil temperatures puff in 4 s and 9 s. What can you conclude if all else was equal?
q.e: Only temperature differed.

q.t: Why is 'scientists don't fully know why a puri puffs' encouraging?
o: Everyday questions can still be open for you to investigate
q.e: Real investigations are possible anywhere.

q.t: Which pair best describes good investigation?
q.e: Root and kite.

q.t: You get an odd result. A good scientist…
q.e: Surprises are worth recording.

q.t: Which is NOT one of the habits worth keeping?
o: Change several things to save time
Vary one thing at a time
q.e: Changing several at once hides the cause.

q.t: Testing 'does dough thickness matter?' needs at least how many different thicknesses to compare?
q.e: You need at least two values to see a difference.

q.t: Why separate what you control from what you measure?
o: So you know what caused what
q.e: Causes go in, results come out.
